summary.name: Service Level Disagreements
summary.one_liner: A 2009 blog post by Benjamin Black arguing that service level agreements (SLAs) are refund policies rather than insurance, so customers should rely on multiple vendors for high availability.
use_cases: evaluating whether a vendor SLA protects against outage losses
planning vendor redundancy for high availability
understanding SLA credit limits versus business impact
reading commentary on cloud service reliability
summary.what_it_does: The post argues that an SLA is not an insurance policy: its maximum payout for a claim is typically the customer's monthly bill, while an outage's real cost to a business can be far higher. It gives an example of a six-hour outage costing a small business 10,000 dollars against a 500 dollar service credit. The author notes that SLA failures become more common higher up the stack, and that outages affecting many customers at once are inevitable in large shared software infrastructure. The post responds to a point by Vijay and a 2008 article by Joe Weinman of AT&T about financial penalties in SLAs. It concludes that the way to achieve availability is to use multiple vendors for the same services, as is common with multihoming and multiple CDNs.
notable: Argues SLAs are refund policies, not insurance hedges
Worked example: 6-hour outage costing 10,000 dollars versus a 500 dollar credit
Recommends multiple vendors for the same service to get high availability
caveats: Opinion essay from 2009; figures and vendor context are dated
Not a tool or product; no software features described
